newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - SISA H1 TO DUCK NEW GAMING WOES.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - SISA H1 TO DUCK NEW GAMING WOES.

text.p: Hotels and leisure group Sun International (Sisa) is seen showing an eight percent rise in half year earnings to December 31, for the moment ducking the ructions of an overhaul of South Africa's gaming industry.

But analysts said on Tuesday the firm, which has now lost its monopoly to run casinos in parts of South Africa, would be hard hit from 1997 by the start-up of competitor operations and cutbacks in its own casinos which new gambling laws demand.

The National Gambling Act passed last year legalises gaming in South Africa for the first time. Under puritanical apartheid laws, the gaming resorts that Sisa ran were tucked away, and flourished, in nominally independent black homelands that Pretoria failed to get the rest of the world to take seriously.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecast earnings to December 31, 1996 rising to between 26 and 29 cents per share with a consensus of 27.8, up 7.8 percent on the six month period a year ago. They expected a dividend of around 15.8 cents from 15 cents when the results are published on February 12.
"None of the problems (for Sisa) have happened yet," an analyst said, explaining that the process of awarding gambling licences had been slow to take off.
"They should have a reasonably stable period for now. It is not until you get out a year hence that the competition starts."

Helen de Goede, an analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak, said Sisa had in the six month period benefitted from a clampdown on illegal gaming operations in the populous Gauteng province which have mushroomed in the past two years.
"But it is very much a balancing out situation. What they benefited from in Gauteng, they lost on the proliferation of illegals down on the coastal regions," she said.

Analysts said results for the six months and for the year would depend largely on how much of its reserves Sisa used to offset its bigger tax bill now that it fell within the South African VAT net and no longer in the zero-rated homeland regime.

According to the gambling act, which makes provision for 40 gaming licences, Sisa will have to rationalise its operations as it holds more than the allowable three licences per province in both the Northwest and Eastern Cape regions. The deadline for the cutbacks is May 1999.

Business Day newspaper reported on Tuesday that Sisa, pre-empting this deadline, was in advanced negotiations to sell or close eight of its resorts -- four in Northwest and four in Eastern Cape -- by the end of this year.
Sisa was not immediately available for comment.

Analysts said the move had been expected and made good business sense as it put Sisa in a stronger position to bid for new licences as they would have substantially reduced the number they currently hold.
"If they do it now they will get it done before their backs are up against the wall...It's a case of if they get a decent offer they will do it," said one analyst.
De Goede said Sisa also had been pushed to act quickly as some of their licences in the Eastern Cape expire in 1997.
